To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) dissimilarity-based methods are a powerful tool for selecting diverse sets of compounds; and (2) dissimilarity matrices can be used to select diverse combinatorial product libraries using either reagent or product-based selection.

(a) the dissimilarity measure is an important component of the diversity selection algorithm, (b) a diversity measure is not required to select a diverse subset from a database, and (c) the diversity measure is not a good predictor of the quality of combinatorial library design.
dissimilarity-based approaches are effective for the selection of diverse sets of compounds from chemical databases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of algorithms and software tools for the design of combinated libraries of compounds.
the development of algorithms for the selection, from large chemical databases, of small, structurally diverse, subsets of compounds that are suitable for combinatorial synthesis.
the development of computational methods for the design of diverse combinatorial chemical libraries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of dissimilarity-based approaches to the selection of combinatorial library designs and the analysis of molecular diversity is an important and promising field of research.
dissimilarity-based methods for the selection of diverse combinatorial library subsets are well-established, efficient, and effective.

the use of dissimilarity measures to identify structurally diverse sets is a promising approach, and that further research is required to develop algorithms for the efficient and effective application of this technique to combinatorial chemistry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the algorithms are simple and fast, and that they can be used to select structurally diverse sets that contain a wide variety of molecular types.
dissimilarity-based methods are very effective for selecting structurally diverse sets.
the algorithms are useful, and they are useful for the design of diverse libraries, but they are not the only useful algorithms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diversity of combinatorial library designs should be measured in the context of the chemical space in which the library will be used.
diversity selection algorithms based on molecular descriptors and molecular fingerprints are not equivalent.
diversity is not just a matter of molecular similarity or dissimilarity.
